newsitem.title: CHINA: Bengang debut charts bleak path for China IPOs.
newsitem.headline: Bengang debut charts bleak path for China IPOs.

text.p: China's B share new issues have lost their allure as a sure-fire investment after Bengang Steel Plates Co Ltd went against tradition with a diving start, analysts said on Wednesday.

Bengang, which on Tuesday became the year's first Shenzhen-listed foreign currency B share to end its initial trading day below the offer price, presaged a bearish tone for new B share offers, they said.
The company's shares fell further on Wednesday, closing down HK$0.15, or 6.38 percent, at HK$2.20, compared with an offer price of HK$2.38.

The steel company's 400 million B share debut stands in stark contrast with earlier new issues on China's southern stock exchange. Wafangdian Bearing Co, Hubei Sanonda Co and Nanjing Posts & Telecommunication Equipment each gained more than 70 percent on their first trading day tis year.

"Bengang's bad performance will have a significant negative impact on new B share issues," Cheng Li, an analyst at China Guotai Securities, told the Hong Kong-based newsletter, the China Securities Bulletin.

Many firms, including Hainan Sundiro Motorcycle, Dalian Refrigeration Equipment Co, Shanghai Zhenhua Port Machinery Co, Zhejiang Southeast Electric Power Co and Inner Mongolia Yitai Coal Co, have said they would list B shares -- supposedly for foreign investors -- later this year.
"Market conditions are worsening," Cheng said. "This means other B share initial public offerings (IPOs) cannot be successful unless they provide lower P/E ratios."
The price/earning ratios of B share offerings so far this year have averaged around 10 times based on 1996 earnings, analysts said.
Bengang's offer implied a P/E of only eight times and poor market conditions have forced some companies to delay their B share offers, they said.

Zhenhua Por was scheduled to launch a 100 million B shareIPO in Shanghai on Tuesday but the issue was put on hold due to falling B share prices, said an official at China Securities Co, the chief domestic underwriter of the issue.
The Shenzhen B share index has fallen roughly 17 percent since last Thursday, the first trading day after Hong Kong returned to Chinese rule on July 1.
Analysts have said the return of the former British colony has removed a bullish psychological factor that had helped buoy share prices earlier in the year.
Shanghai's B share index has also fallen sharply albeit with a rebound on Wednesday.
"The curtain has just been raised on B share market expansion, but it is not very successful so far," Cheng said.
Shenzhen has listed six B shares so far this year and Shanghai has listed three, analysts said.
Waning investor confidence is also threatening Beijing's ambitious expansion plan for A shares aimed at domestic investors, they said.
The government has announced 30 billion yuan worth of new A share quota for 1997, doubling the 15 billon yuan for 1996. Analysts said some of the 1996 quota has yet to be used.
"The potential profits for A share IPO subscribers are shrinking, which will dampen investor enthusiasm," said Wang Feng, an analyst at Shenzhen J&A Securities.
On average, A shares listed this month rose 50-100 percent on their first day of trading, compared with about 200 percent for those listed in the first quarter of this year, analysts said.

They said this reflected moves by China's market regulators to curb wild swings in prices with measures that included a ban on state banks, state enterprises and listed firms from speculating on the markets.
